title: Admin session cookie without SameSite/CSRF token is NOT exploitable cross-site (browser Lax default blocks the POST sinks)
description: The code configures the session cookie with only { maxAge } (plus secure=false in production) and never sets SameSite, and the admin API auth chain relies solely on the signed 'asid' cookie read in [context]getCurrentUser.ts:24 with no CSRF token/Origin/Referer check (confirmed by grep: no SameSite attribute, no csrf library, no origin/referrer middleware anywhere in src). The session is the only ambient-identity control.
claimed_root_cause: Session-cookie-only auth with no SameSite attribute, no CSRF token, and no Origin/Referer binding; the only same-site defense is the browser default.

trace.description: express-session mounted as adminSessionMiddleware; cookie object sets only maxAge (78-83), forces secure=false in production (85-88); SameSite is never set. REJECTED premise: for POST-only endpoints the browser Lax default (SameSite unset) prevents cross-site cookie attachment.
cookie option { maxAge: 24h } only; no SameSite/secure override. Same default semantics.

Identity derives solely from request.signedCookies['asid']; with SameSite=Lax the asid cookie is NOT sent on cross-site POST, so getCurrentUser returns null and the sink is gated off before any handler.

POST /orders/:id/capture reads only request.params.id, no body; but it is POST-only and private - the Lax-default cookie is not attached to cross-site POST, so the capture never authenticates and cannot be reached cross-site.

evidence.description: cookie: { maxAge: ... } only; no sameSite - SameSite attribute absent, browser Lax default applies.
sess.cookie.secure = false in production; no SameSite=Strict/None, no SameSite override anywhere.
cookie: { maxAge } only; same Lax-default semantics.
request.signedCookies[asid] is the sole session identifier; no SameSite=None config and no Origin/Referer check exist in the auth chain.
POST-only route; Lax default would not send asid on a cross-site POST.
POST-only route; multipart upload is POST, also blocked by Lax default.

reason: Independent Phase 5 verification refuted the cross-site exploit: the repo never sets SameSite on the session cookie (only maxAge plus secure=false in production), so browsers apply the default SameSite=Lax, which does NOT attach the cookie to cross-site POST requests. Every claimed state-changing sink (POST /api/orders/:id/capture, POST /api/files/* and multipart upload) is POST-only and unreachable cross-site regardless of the absence of CSRF tokens or Origin checks. The 'secure=false in production' and missing-SameSite conditions remain credible hardening/defense-in-depth notes (cookie flags should be explicit for transit/storage hardening and any future GET-state-changing surface), but the asserted cross-boundary CSRF result is not actionable and the claim is rejected rather than recorded as needs_validation.

title: Public cart/order APIs and storefront GraphQL bind carts only by client-supplied uuid (missing object-level ownership check, IDOR)
description: The storefront exposes cart operations (POST /api/orders placeOrder.js, POST /api/carts/:cart_id/items addItemToCart.js, /api/graphql Query.cart) that locate a cart solely via a client-supplied uuid. getCartByUUID() is a thin passthrough of the caller's uuid into getCart(), whose only predicates are uuid = ? and status = true (Cart.js:185-186). No handler on this path ever compares the cart's sid/customer_id to the requester's session/customer; the API routes skip express-session middleware entirely ('Restful api should be stateless', addDefaultMiddlewareFuncs.ts:224-225), so there is no server-side ownership binding to enforce. The guestCheckout gate in orderValidator.ts:117 authenticates the cart row's persisted customer_id (written earlier by [auth]addCustomerToCart for the sid's owner), never the acting principal, so a caller who cites a known active cart uuid passes the gate and createOrder()/saveOrder() (orderCreator.ts:139-152) writes an order row from the victim cart's customer_email/customer_full_name/addresses/items and disables that cart (line 216). GraphQL Query.cart resolves the full cart (customerEmail, customerFullName, userIp, shipping/billing addresses, items) with no context-based ownership logic (Cart.resolvers.ts:19-26). The intended pattern is demonstrated by the scoped siblings getMyCart.ts:17-51, Query.myCart, Customer.orders (Order.resolvers.js:148-156), and the addMine*/updateMine*/removeMine* REST endpoints, all of which bind to the session/customer identity. Confirmed: no ownership comparison exists anywhere on the public cart path. Strong counterweight: cart uuid is PostgreSQL gen_random_uuid (122-bit), so the capability is unguessable; the cross-customer impact requires a uuid-leak channel, and the actual exploitation of a live instance cannot be observed without a runtime environment.
claimed_root_cause: getCartByUUID()/getCart() bind a cart only by uuid (plus the status flag) - no sid/customer ownership predicate in the loader, no requester-vs-cart identity comparison in any public caller - and the guestCheckout authorization gate asserts on the cart's persisted customer_id instead of the acting principal (orderValidator.ts:117), so a known active cart uuid acts as a bearer capability for cross-customer read (Query.cart), mutation (addCartItem/saveContactInfo/checkout), and order placement (POST /api/orders).

trace.description: POST /api/orders (route.json access public). cart_id is read from request.body (line 16) and passed verbatim to getCartByUUID(cart_id) (line 18); the only guards are cart existence and cart.hasError() (lines 19-38), then createOrder(cart) is invoked at line 40. No requester-vs-cart ownership comparison.

/graphql served with access public; route is under the api/ tree so it is mounted at /api/graphql, isApi=true, and therefore skips express-session middleware. Storefront schema is built by buildTypes.js:17-21 which ignores only '*.admin.graphql', so Cart.graphql's non-admin defs (including 'extend type Query { cart(id: String!): Cart }' at Cart.graphql:200-202) enter the public schema.
Thin passthrough (lines 9-11): takes only uuid, forwards unmodified to getCart. No sid/customer parameter.

getCart(uuid) selects from 'cart' where uuid = $1 and throws only when the row is missing or status !== true (lines 185-188); the returned Cart carries persisted customer_id, customer_email, customer_full_name, user_ip, sid, addresses and items, all of which exportData() exposes.

Query.cart(id) calls getCartByUUID(id) and returns camelCase(cart.exportData()) (lines 21-22) with no session/customer context used; the scoped sibling Query.myCart (lines 27-48) uses getMyCart(sessionID, customer_id).

guestCheckout validator: if getAllowGuestCheckout() is false, gate is Boolean(cart.getData('customer_id')) - it authenticates the persisted customer_id on the cart row (bound earlier to the sid's owner), never the acting principal, so citing another customer's active cart uuid passes the gate (default guest config is true, checkoutSettings.ts:16).

POST /api/carts/:cart_id/items (route.json access public): loads cart by getCartByUUID(cartId) from request.params, adds the requested SKU and saveCart() - uuid-only mutation of whatever cart the caller names.

saveOrder() inserts into 'order' with {...cart.exportData(), ...} (lines 139-152) from the victim-owned cart state, and createOrderFunc then disables the referenced cart via disableCart (line 216; update status=false at 68-74), in the same transaction as validation.

evidence.description: select().from('cart').where('uuid','=',uuid).load(pool); line 186 throws only if !cart || cart.status !== true - uuid+status are the entire predicate.
export const getCartByUUID = async (uuid: string) => { return getCart(uuid); } - no identity parameter.
Sibling scoped loader: selects cart where status=1 AND sid=sessionID, else where customer_id=customerId (lines 18-22, 31-35) - the ownership binding absent from the getCartByUUID path.
cart = await getCartByUUID(cart_id) from request.body; createOrder(cart) at line 40.
"access": "public" for POST /orders.

sessionMiddleware: if (currentRoute?.isApi || !routeNeedsSession(...)) next(); line 225 comment 'We don't need session for api routes. Restful api should be stateless.' API routes (all checkout/api + /api/graphql) get no server-side session binding.
if (currentRoute?.access === 'public') { next(); return; } - 401 applies only to private routes; all cited cart endpoints are public.
guestCheckout validator block (104-120); gate at 117 returns Boolean(cart.getData('customer_id')) on the persisted cart row, not on the acting principal.
await hookable(disableCart, { cart })(cart.getData('cart_id'), connection); disableCart() at 68-74 sets cart.status=false - the victim's cart is consumed by an attacker-picked order.
Query.cart resolver uses only the client-supplied id (no context.customer/sid check); Query.myCart at 27-48 is the scoped sibling.

Cart type exposes customerId/customerGroupId/customerEmail/customerFullName/userIp/userId (162-167), shippingAddress (159), billingAddress (160) and items (157); extend type Query { cart(id: String!): Cart } at 200-202.

Writes customer_group_id, customer_id, customer_full_name, customer_email onto the sid-bound cart (18-26) - this persisted identity is later asserted by the guestCheckout gate instead of the requester.
POST /api/carts/:cart_id/contacts (route.json access public): uuid-only load, then cart.setData('customer_email', email) at line 24 + saveCart.
setContextValue(request, 'cartId', cart.getData('uuid')) and response cartId at line 102 - cart uuid handed to the client-visible API response.
POST /api/carts/:cart_id/items with "access": "public" (line 4).

cartCheckout also loads by getCartByUUID(cartId) only (line 16); the current requester's identity is then written over the order's customer fields (checkout.ts:22-31) without ever verifying the requester owns the uuid-referenced cart - the same identity confusion on the parallel /api/carts/:cart_id/checkout path (also public).
Customer.orders is scoped: select from 'order' where order.customer_id = customerId (149-153) - the intended order ownership binding (Order.graphql:199-201).
cart table: "uuid" UUID NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() - the cart capability is a 122-bit random token, so cross-customer impact depends on uuid acquisition, not enumeration.
isApi routes are mounted at /api/<path> (line 47) - confirms all cited route.json files under checkout/api land on the stateless /api surface.

getAllowGuestCheckout() defaults to true (getConfig('checkout.allowGuestCheckout', true)), so the /api/orders gate passes without logging in, leaving only the persisted customer_id gate as the (bypassed) control.

blockers: Decisive runtime fact unobservable from source or local run: whether an anonymous or unrelated HTTP client can successfully reach an active victim cart's data/operations on a live deployment using only a known cart uuid. No sandbox is available and deployed endpoints must not be contacted.

Secondary runtime dependency: cart uuids are gen_random_uuid (122-bit), so exploitation presupposes a uuid-leak channel (shared checkout links, client-side JSON/url exposure, referrer/history, logs, support screenshots); whether the deployed storefront actually leaks active cart uuids to a second party cannot be determined from repository source alone.
The order-placement leg additionally assumes a checkout-ready victim cart (non-empty, validated; guest checkout default true) - confirmable on a live fixtures instance, not statically.

validation_plan.local: Boot a throwaway local instance at this commit (postgres migrations up, dev server). As an anonymous client: create cart A in session X (POST /api/carts), add an item, set contact info (POST /api/carts/A/contacts). Then in an unrelated session Y (different/no cookies): (1) GET/POST /api/graphql with query { cart(id: A) { customerEmail customerFullName shippingAddress { fullName address1 } } } and assert it returns cart A's PII while myCart returns null in session Y; (2) POST /api/carts/A/items and assert it mutates cart A from an unauthenticated client; (3) POST /api/orders with { cart_id: A } and assert an order row is created from cart A's state and cart A status flips to false; and (4) repeat via the scoped siblings (POST /api/carts/me/items, query myCart) and assert they do NOT reach cart A. Read-only GraphQL assertions first; mutations only against throwaway fixtures; tear everything down after.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner replicates the same fixture in a staging instance of commit 18e02022631c1c9dba1b6e5ac734ae27b54632cb (NODE_ENV=production) and, from a separate host/IP with no storefront session cookie, confirms: read of cart A PII via public Query.cart; item mutation of cart A via the public REST cart endpoints; order placement from cart A via POST /api/orders (and/or /api/carts/A/checkout), including the disableCart side-effect on cart A; optionally set checkout.allowGuestCheckout=false and confirm the gate remains satisfied by cart A's persisted customer_id. Report only on the operator's own fixtures; no production data touched.

title: Upload mimetype allowlist trusts the client-declared Content-Type, letting script-capable files (e.g. SVG) be stored in media and served to storefront visitors
description: The CMS upload allowlist is the only control separating attacker payload from stored, served content, and it is a label check. getMulter.js states the explicit intent that SVG must never be storable because SVGs 'can carry scripts and are an XSS vector when served' (lines 7-10), yet fileFilter accepts a file solely on getAllowedMimeTypes().includes(file.mimetype) (lines 157-163), where file.mimetype is the value multer/busboy derives from the multipart part's client-supplied Content-Type header (verification requires runtime — multer/busboy are not vendored). No magic-byte/content sniffing exists anywhere on the write path. An authenticated admin (POST /api/files/* and /api/images/* are access:private, gated by the auth/api/global [getCurrentUser]auth middleware that requires an admin user) can therefore upload SVG/HTML-carrying bytes with a declared Content-Type of image/png and a filename evil.svg; the imageUpload variant merely re-tests the same client-declared string via file.mimetype.startsWith('image'). generateFileName preserves the client-supplied extension, and localUploader (uploadFile.ts:85) writes the buffer verbatim under CONSTANTS.MEDIAPATH. The storefront GET /assets/* route (static.ts) then serves any MEDIAPATH file whose extension is in ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS — which includes '.svg' (line 16) — to anonymous visitors with only X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and cache headers; the stored .svg is therefore an active-content resource on the store origin. The affected principal is the anonymous storefront visitor (stored XSS on direct/iframe navigation or embedding of the served .svg); the planting principal is an admin or anybody holding an admin token.
claimed_root_cause: The content-based enforcement that the allowlist claims to provide is actually a declaration check: fileFilter accepts when getAllowedMimeTypes().includes(file.mimetype), where file.mimetype is derived from the untrusted multipart-part Content-Type, and the resulting bytes are stored un-inspected (CustomMemoryStorage buffer written verbatim by localUploader) under the client-chosen file extension, which static.ts allowlists for anonymous serving (including .svg).

trace.description: POST /files/* declared access:private, gated by the API auth middleware (auth/api/global/[getCurrentUser]auth.ts:18,23-31) which returns 401 unless an admin user session/JWT (roles '*' or matching) is present; middleware sort positions 'auth' before multerFile.

After the path regex gate (lines 5-13), getMulter().array('images', 20)(...) runs multer over the multipart body; storage is CustomMemoryStorage, whose _handleFile buffers the part stream and calls this.getFilename(file.originalname).

fileFilter accepts a file iff getAllowedMimeTypes().includes(file.mimetype); file.mimetype is the multipart-part client-declared type and is the sole decision input — no content/magic-byte inspection exists on the path.
path.extname(file.originalname) is preserved and appended, so a stored file can end in the attacker-chosen .svg extension while the declared mimetype is image/png.
localUploader.upload writes file.buffer verbatim to path.join(CONSTANTS.MEDIAPATH, destinationPath, file.filename) — bytes are never re-inspected or transcoded on the write path.

Storefront GET /assets/* reaches the media branch (lines 130-137): if join(MEDIAPATH, path) exists and its extension is in ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS — '.svg' is at line 16 — serve-static responds with only X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and cache headers set; no CSP or content-types restriction.

evidence.description: fileFilter(request, file, cb) accepts iff getAllowedMimeTypes().includes(file.mimetype); file.mimetype is the client-declared multipart part type and the sole decision input (function at 157, decision at 158).

Header comment and DEFAULT_ALLOWED_MIME_TYPES (lines 11-18) state SVG is deliberately excluded because SVGs 'can carry scripts and are an XSS vector when served' — the invariant the allowlist intends but does not enforce against content.
const extension = path.extname(originalname) — the stored file extension is taken from the client-supplied originalname, so a file declared as image/png can still be stored as evil.svg.
The image-route variant rejects only files where !file.mimetype.startsWith('image') — a re-test of the same client-declared string, not of the bytes.

'.svg' is in ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS, and lines 130-137 serve any existing MEDIAPATH file whose extension is allowlisted, to anonymous visitors at /assets/media/..., setting only X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff plus cache headers.

blockers: Runtime/provenance of file.mimetype: confirming that multer/busboy sets file.mimetype verbatim from the client's multipart part Content-Type header requires executing a bounded multipart POST against getMulter() in an OS-enforced sandbox fixture (multer ^2.2.0/busboy are declared dependencies, not vendored in this source-only clone, so their behavior is not locally observable).

Served semantics: confirming that serve-static (^1.15.0, not vendored) answers /assets/media/.svg with Content-Type image/svg+xml and that the SVG scripts execute on direct/iframe navigation (whereas embedding does not run them) requires a local browser/render check against a dummy store on loopback.

Reachability precondition: the private /api/files and /api/images endpoints require an admin credential; whether an attacker-usable admin token is obtainable depends on peer-verified auth findings (e.g. JWT-mint rate-limit tier) and their runtime confirmation.

validation_plan.local: In an OS-enforced sandbox (no network, empty env, low CPU/mem/disk, scratch-only writes), run the existing unittest harness (packages/evershop/src/modules/cms/api/fileUpload/tests/unit) or a bounded jest/multer fixture that POSTs a multipart body with part header Content-Type: image/png whose bytes are <svg><script>...</script></svg> and filename evil.svg; assert fileFilter passes and CustomMemoryStorage yields a buffer of the SVG bytes. Then serve that stored file through lib/middlewares/static.ts's serve-static handler on isolated loopback and capture the response Content-Type header and body bytes for the combination content-type:image/png (part header) + evil.svg (part filename), and confirm an anonymous GET /assets/media/... reaches the media serve branch.
validation_plan.deployment: Confirm the admin session/JWT protection of /api/files and /api/images in the target deployment, confirm the storefront /assets/* route is reachable anonymously at the store origin, and confirm no edge WAF/content-inspection strips or blocks the stored .svg (or blocks admin-authored absolute URLs such as <a href="/assets/media/evil.svg">) before the visitor-visible result is assessed.

title: Public /images endpoint writes unbounded, never-evicted derivative files keyed by attacker-chosen width/height/quality/format
description: GET /images is public and session-free: route.json registers the route with no access/auth field, and routeNeedsSession.ts (SESSION_EXEMPT_ROUTE_IDS) plus its unit test explicitly exempt route id 'images' so no session is created. It is only subject to the page-tier per-IP rate limit (300 req/60s, rateLimit.ts) because path /images matches no STATIC_ASSET extension, no auth POST path, and no /api/ prefix. images.ts:11-21 passes attacker-controlled width = parseInt(q.w,10) (no min/max clamp; only NaN/0 filtered), optional unbounded height, quality = parseInt(q.q)||75 (unbounded), and one of an allowlisted 4-value format set into imageProcessor. generateCacheKey (imageProcessor.ts:33-46) builds a distinct filename for every (src,width,height,quality,format,upscale) tuple from untrusted input, with no clamp on any numeric dimension. Every cache miss runs the full sharp decode+resize+encode pipeline (imageProcessor.ts:289-368) and unconditionally fs.writeFile's the result into CACHE_DIR = path.resolve(BUILDPATH,'../images') = <root>/.evershop/images (imageProcessor.ts:174,177-181,371-372). withoutEnlargement (line 295) and sharp's default pixel caps bound each individual FILE's size (widths above source width still write an approximately source-sized derivative under a distinct key) but nothing bounds the NUMBER of retained files: a grep of the whole tree finds no eviction, TTL, aggregate file-count/byte cap, or cleanup owner for .evershop/images (the build-time rmSync of .evershop/build does not touch the parent images dir; the unit suite's beforeEach only clears root/media/cache and explicitly leaves the derivative outputs in place). One accessible source image (any media/public/theme file; product/category image srcs are emitted as public /images?src=... URLs by productView, categoryView, PageInfo, emailHelper) yields an unbounded set of persistent, NSD-served files. Impact is persistent growth on the shared app disk volume (filling it stops the whole storefront) plus per-miss CPU/IO. The only control is the per-IP page-tier limiter; concurrency is not capped and distributed sources are not bounded. Source trace and scope are fully re-verified and match the repo; the decisive runtime observations (real sharp retained-write behavior, per-file byte projection, key-space regions that error, and whether an operator edge caps /images) remain outside source-only observation.
claimed_root_cause: The derivative cache is keyed by an unbounded arithmetic manifold from untrusted query parameters (width/height/quality/format), is written on every miss with fs.writeFile to <root>/.evershop/images, and has no cardinality/aggregate bound, no eviction, and no TTL anywhere in the tree — a unique-cache-keys-without-aggregate-limits failure (unbounded buffering/cardinality) reachable without authentication.

trace.description: route.json registers methods GET on path /images with no access field and no auth middleware; routeNeedsSession.ts:9-13 (verified here) lists route id 'images' in SESSION_EXEMPT_ROUTE_IDS, so the session middleware skips it (addDefaultMiddlewareFuncs.ts:222-237) and responses carry no session cookie.

width = parseInt(request.query.w,10), height = parseInt(...) optionally, quality = parseInt(request.query.q)||75 (line 16), and format from a 4-value allowlist (lines 17-21) are all attacker-controlled; the only filters (lines 23-30) are missing src, missing/NaN/zero width, and NaN height — no numeric clamp upstream.
generateCacheKey (lines 33-46) embeds base64url(src)-widthw[-heighth][-up]-qualityq.format into the filename, so every distinct untrusted (src,w,h,q,f) tuple maps to a distinct persistent cache key.

On every cache miss the full sharp pipeline executes (decode, resize with withoutEnlargement at line 295, encode to the chosen format, lines 306-368); a failed pipeline throws and is caught at line 387, so only sharp-processable sources retain files.

fs.writeFile(finalCachedImagePath, optimizedImageBuffer) persists each distinct derivative into CACHE_DIR = path.resolve(BUILDPATH,'../images') -> <root>/.evershop/images (line 174, mkdir recursive at lines 177-181); no eviction, TTL, or count/byte cap exists anywhere in the repo.

evidence.description: generateCacheKey embeds width, height, quality, and format from untrusted input into the cache filename; the key space is unbounded because images.ts applies no min/max clamp to w/h/q and only allowlists the 4-value format.

CACHE_DIR = path.resolve(CONSTANTS.BUILDPATH, '../images') with BUILDPATH = <root>/.evershop/build (helpers.ts:23) resolves to <root>/.evershop/images, lazily mkdir'd (lines 177-181) and appended to forever on every miss (line 372).

withoutEnlargement: !allowUpscale bounds each output FILE's pixels to the source (public route never sets allowUpscale), but no code bounds how many distinct keys are created or retained; widths above source width still write an approximately source-sized file per key.

quality = parseInt(request.query.q)||75 accepts any positive integer value; combined with unbounded w/h, the derived key space is an unbounded arithmetic manifold over a fixed bounded set of source images.

blockers: No OS sandbox: demonstrating the effective disk/cardinality growth (that N distinct (src,w,h,q,f) tuples with a real sharp pipeline each dry-write N retained files, measured per-file bytes, and that a bounded per-IP budget still fills an operator-plausible volume) requires a bounded local fixture this environment explicitly cannot run.

Sharp/library behavior for extreme, negative, or absurd w/h/q values (which keys error and thus stay dry vs succeed and retain files) is external to the repo and needs a pinned-version runtime fixture to establish.

Deployed topology: the page-tier per-IP rate limit (300/60s, express-rate-limit MemoryStore, bucketed via TRUST_PROXY_HOPS) may bound single-source growth, but whether multi-source/concurrency pressure, autoscaling/replica count, or a CDN/WAF actually caps /images, and whether the hosting volume is shared with logging/media stores, are deployment facts that decide the achievable retained-growth impact.

validation_plan.local: In a strict OS sandbox (no egress, scratch-only writes onto a small temporary volume, low disk/mem/time limits), drive the /images handler (or imageProcessor directly, as packages/evershop/src/modules/cms/services/tests/unit/imageProcessor.test.js does with a scratch root, committed media/ fixtures, and a scratch images/ BUILDPATH) through a handful of distinct (w,h,q,f) tuples and assert (a) each miss returns a distinct file under the scratch CACHE_DIR, (b) the cache directory grows monotonically with tuple count and no call ever triggers cleanup, and (c) which extreme/negative w/h/q keys error instead of writing (dry regions of the key space). Then measure per-file byte sizes to extrapolate whether a bounded per-IP request budget (300/min) over a long run, or distributed sources, fills an operator-plausible shared volume.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner should check the deployed <root>/.evershop/images directory size and file count over a production window, confirm whether that volume is shared with logging/media stores, and verify whether the edge (Cloudflare WAF/rate-limit or equivalent) actually caps /images beyond the in-app per-IP page-tier limiter before accepting this as a confirmed service-availability impact.

title: Image pipeline disables pixel caps for SVG rasterization and buffers unbounded external-fetch bodies on a public endpoint
description: Two representation-amplification paths in the same handler are reachable without authentication through GET /images (public route, no session per addDefaultMiddlewareFuncs.ts; only the page-tier 300/60s-per-IP rate limit applies): (1) any source buffer sharp classifies as SVG is rasterized with density:300 and limitInputPixels:false (imageProcessor.ts:306-313), removing sharp's default ~268MP input pixel cap, so an SVG declaring a very large canvas decodes to a huge unbounded raster even when the requested w/h is small (the resize at line 313 is applied only after full rasterization); for jpeg output an SVG is re-rasterized to png (imageProcessor.ts:274-277); (2) for an allowlisted external source, secureFetch enforces only a 15s timeout (secureFetch.ts:3,126) with no response-body size cap, and imageProcessor buffers the entire body via response.arrayBuffer() (imageProcessor.ts:228-229) before sharp's capped decode. Both convert one bounded request into arbitrarily large CPU/memory work on the shared service (sharp runs on the libuv pool; buffered bodies sit in Node heap). Both paths require a condition outside default deployments: an SVG must exist in a locally readable location (media/public/theme — the default pools ship none) or on an allowlisted host, and the external path further requires the operator to have configured IMAGE_ALLOWED_HOSTS / a matching storage provider host whose objects a caller can point at with a large body. The unit-1 mimetype-based upload check (verifyImages trusts the client-claimed mimetype) is a compounding precondition for planting an SVG in media.
claimed_root_cause: sharp is asked to rasterize SVG without limitInputPixels (deliberately disabled at imageProcessor.ts:312) at an elevated density (300), and external fetch responses are buffered in full with no byte cap (secureFetch.ts:126 only sets a 15s timeout, and imageProcessor.ts:228 uses response.arrayBuffer()), i.e. the decoded/buffered representation size is not bounded at decode/buffer time.

trace.description: Public GET /images with attacker-chosen src (local media/public/theme path or external URL on the allowlist), width, optional height, quality, and one of 4 formats; unauthenticated (route.json methods GET; session middleware exempts /images).
External branch: secureFetch(src) then response.arrayBuffer() with no size check before decode.

SVG branch: sharp(sourceImageBuffer, { density: 300, limitInputPixels: false }) disables the default input pixel cap and raises rasterization density; full raster is materialized before the bounded resize.
The fully-decoded/buffered representation is then resized/encoded — the output is bounded only after the unbounded decode/buffer already occurred.
Only a 15s AbortController timeout (REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS=15000, defined at line 3) bounds the undici fetch; no maxBytes/maxContentLength is supplied, so the response body is unbounded.

evidence.description: limitInputPixels: false on the SVG sharp configuration removes the default ~268MP input cap for the attacker-relevant SVG class.
const arrayBuffer = await response.arrayBuffer() buffers the whole external body with no cap enforced by secureFetch.
REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS=15000 (line 3) feeds a setTimeout(abort) here — the only curl-side bound on the external fetch; body size is unbounded.
SVG content with format==='jpeg' is re-processed to png, so the unbounded SVG raster happens even when the requested output format is jpeg.

blockers: Whether a hostile SVG exists in any readable location in the deployed store (default media/public/theme pools ship none; the unit-1 mimetype-based upload bypass is a needed precondition unless the operator allows SVG hosts) is a deployment/condition fact that source cannot settle.

title: Login credential lookup escapes only '%' in the ILIKE pattern, leaving '_' as a wildcard
description: Both login lookups (admin via loginUserWithEmail, storefront via loginCustomerWithEmail) build the email predicate with PostgreSQL ILIKE after escaping only '%' (email.replace(/%/g,'\\%')), leaving '_' as a single-char wildcard. A login for a_b@example.com therefore also matches acb@example.com, a1b@example.com, etc. Because .load() appends LIMIT 0,1 with no ORDER BY and returns the first row, a multi-row ILIKE match can select an arbitrary account; if the supplied password matches that returned row (e.g. password reuse / guessed common password), the session/token is bound to a different account. Impact is bounded because a matching password for the selected row is still required, but exact-match account-selection semantics are violated on both the admin and customer credential paths.
claimed_root_cause: The login services escape only the '%' metacharacter before the ILIKE comparison; '_' (and any backslash) are left active as ILIKE wildcard metacharacters. title: Password-reset token travels and is rendered as a URL query parameter with no Referrer-Policy cap
description: The reset flow mints a 128-hex token (crypto.randomBytes(64).toString('hex')), emails it as ${getBaseUrl()}/account/reset-password?token=<token>, and the storefront page reads the token back out of window.location.search and renders it into a hidden form input in the DOM. The application sets no Referrer-Policy header (its only security header is X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff on static assets), so the token stays live in the URL for the lifetime of the page: it persists in browser history, in server/proxy/CDN access logs for the page GET and for any same-origin navigation, and is subject to mail-client link prefetch. Cross-origin Referer leakage depends on the deployment's effective Referrer-Policy/browser defaults: modern defaults (strict-origin-when-cross-origin) strip the query string for cross-origin requests, so the specific 'an external-link click forwards the full token via Referer' mechanism is weaker than the hunter's wording suggests, but history/log/DOM exposure is not policy-dependent. The token is sha256-hashed at rest, single-use (deleted after consumption), and 48h-bounded, so the window is time-boxed.
claimed_root_cause: The reset token is delivered as a URL query parameter and re-read from window.location.search on the client, and the application emits no Referrer-Policy (or equivalent) response header to cap where that URL may propagate; the token is also rendered into a hidden form input in the DOM.

On mount the page reads the token from the URL: const tokenParam = urlParams.get('token') from new URLSearchParams(window.location.search), keeping the secret addressable in history and page state.

<InputField name="token" type="hidden" defaultValue={token} /> renders the token into the page DOM; a same-origin script or XSS would read it, and it is submitted to POST /customers/password on reset.

Consumption endpoint re-hashes the submitted token and requires the row's created_at >= (now - resetPasswordTokenLifetime, default 48h), then deletes the row (lines 63-69), enforcing single-use and a 48h window.

title: Session ID is never rotated on login and never destroyed on logout; raw sid is returned in login bodies
description: loginUserWithEmail and loginCustomerWithEmail write userID/customerID into the existing (possibly anonymous) session without session.regenerate(); logoutUser and logoutCustomer only null the property and session.save() the same sid (no destroy()). adminLoginJson and customerLoginJson return request.sessionID in the response $body, which the page response handler sends verbatim to the client. Sets this.session.customerID = customer.customer_id on the existing session object with no session.regenerate().
After login, this.session.save(callback) persists the mutated session under the unchanged sid assigned for it.
Logout only sets this.session.userID = undefined (no session.destroy()/regenerate()); bootstrap then session.save()s the same sid, which stays valid and reusable.
Logout only sets this.session.customerID = undefined (no destroy/regenerate); the same sid survives on the server.

title: Storefront rich-text image blocks render an unsanitized 'link' as an anchor href (catalog product/category/collection descriptions)

title: Storefront SSR preview/schedule-windowed responses set no Cache-Control or noindex and emit the real canonical URL — draft/out-of-window landing page content can be served at the canonical URL from an external cache
description: Landing pages (promotion/pages/frontStore/landingPageView/index.ts) are live only when status=true AND within the publish window (publish_start/publish_end); a draft or out-of-window page 404s unless a valid ?changeset=<token> is supplied, which renders the draft/out-of-window content at the REAL canonical /<key> URL with full title/description meta. Verified in source: line 44 loads landing_page without a status filter; lines 55-64 compute isLive = status AND isWithinSchedule, isPreview = !isLive AND isValidPreviewToken(?changeset); lines 77-85 call setPageMetaInfo with canonicalUrl = getBaseUrl() + localizeUrl('/' + url_key) for BOTH live and preview renders, and HeadTags.tsx:112 emits <link rel="canonical" href={canonicalUrl}>. title: Untrusted storefront GraphQL queries are parsed and executed without document validation or depth/complexity/alias bounds (computational amplification on the shared DB pool)
description: The storefront GraphQL endpoint (route.json path /graphql, mounted by scanForRoutes.js as /api/graphql, access 'public') is processed by graphqlMiddleware, which parses the attacker-supplied document (parse(query) with no token/size options), calls validateSchema(schema, document) — an API that validates the SCHEMA object and ignores the document argument, so the query AST is never validated and graphql-js specifiedRules are never applied — and then executes the raw AST with no depth, complexity, alias, or introspection limit. The storefront schema is self-referential (Category.children/parent/path at Category.graphql lines 17-19) and Category.children/parent/hasChildren execute one DB select per resolved node (Category.resolvers.ts:124-136, 168-182), and list/cards resolvers issue per-row queries, so a single sub-100kB unauthenticated POST can multiply into thousands of DB statements against the shared all-tenant Postgres pool and event loop, even by pure alias fan-out independent of catalog depth. Per-IP rate limiting (api tier 120 req/60 s, rateLimit.ts:20) and body-parser.json's default ~100 kB cap bound request volume and input size but not the per-request amplification factor. Introspection (__schema/__type) remains enabled. Because larger/aliased documents can be delivered ratably across many IPs and there is no per-request cleanup step, the result is untrusted-work-driven, unauthenticated, cross-tenant CPU/DB load.
claimed_root_cause: graphql/services/graphqlMiddleware.js:22 uses the wrong validation API (validateSchema(schema, document) instead of validate(schema, document, rules)), so graphql-js specifiedRules are never applied to the attacker document; execute() is invoked without operation-complexity, depth, or alias caps while the schema contains recursive types (Category.children/parent/path) whose resolvers perform per-node database selects and per-row list queries.

trace.description: route.json declares path /graphql, methods GET|POST, access 'public'; scanForRoutes.js prefixes '/api' for api routes, so /api/graphql is registered unauthenticated.
parse(query) runs with no options; pinned graphql 16.12.0 parse defaults impose no token/length caps, so the attacker AST is fully materialized.

validateSchema(schema, document) validates the schema object, not the request document; the query AST is never validated and specifiedRules are never run, so malformed, deep, or alias-heavy documents are never rejected.
execute({schema, contextValue, document, variableValues}) applies no depth/complexity/alias limits and introspection fields remain resolvable.
Category is self-referential via children: [Category], parent: Category, path: [Category] (lines 17-19), so structural recursion in a query is bounded only by the request document length.
children executes a DB select against the shared pool per fetched category node (line 134); deep nesting, parent chains, and alias fan-out multiply per-node DB work multiplicatively.

evidence.description: validateSchema(schema, document) — the argument document is ignored by graphql-js validateSchema; validationErrors stays empty for any syntactically parseable query, so no document validation occurs.

execute() called without any operation-complexity/depth/alias limits; no rule list or custom validation rule is applied anywhere in modules/graphql (grep confirms no validate/specifiedRules/depth/complexity usage on this path except the SSR twin).
access 'public' — [getCurrentUser]auth.ts:18-21 short-circuits to next() for public routes, so no authentication gate precedes query execution.

children: [Category], parent: Category, path: [Category] (lines 17-19) allow unbounded nesting in the storefront schema; corresponding resolvers (Category.resolvers.ts:124-167) issue per-node DB selects.

api tier limits 120 requests / 60 s per IP (rateLimit.ts:20) and /api/graphql classifies as the api tier; this bounds request volume, not per-request amplification — a single 100 kB body-parser.json document can carry thousands of aliases.

Deployed topology is unknown: whether any CDN/WAF/API gateway imposes GraphQL operation depth/complexity/alias caps in front of /api/graphql is not source-visible.

title: Order cancellation unconditionally restocks full ordered quantities, ignoring manage_stock and shipped/delivered amounts, and the reStockAfterCancellation option is never honored
description: cancelOrder restocks the full order_item.qty for every item of a canceled order without the `manage_stock = TRUE` guard the placement-time deduction trigger applies, without subtracting already-shipped/delivered quantities, and regardless of the `oms.order.reStockAfterCancellation` config (registered in oms/bootstrap.ts, default true, never read in core). title: Concurrent capture requests can both pass the isCapturable gate and invoke the gateway settle twice
description: captureOrder loads the order with a plain, lockless SELECT (captureOrder.ts:38-41), gates on isCapturable by reading that in-memory payment_status (63), selects the authorization transaction without a lock (71-79), calls factory.capture -- the one gateway settle, network I/O -- and only afterwards records the capture (insertOnUpdate at 95) and flips payment_status (updatePaymentStatus at 113) inside a short transaction. Because the gate is not a conditional state transition and no per-order advisory lock is taken (contrast pg_advisory_xact_lock at createShipment.ts:90), two concurrent POST /orders/:id/capture requests can both observe the authorized status and both invoke the gateway settle on the same authorization before either records. Both ledger writes commit: for a reused gateway id the unique-key insert collapses to the same row via ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE (postgres-query-builder index.ts:1134; UNQ_PAYMENT_TRANSACTION_ID_ORDER_ID in checkout migration), while a PayPal capture mints a fresh capture id and inserts a second row; whoever commits last simply overwrites payment_status. Whether a second settle actually moves funds is external to core and depends on the provider adapter's idempotency.
claimed_root_cause: The capture gate is a non-atomic check-then-act: order.payment_status is read into memory (captureOrder.ts:38-41) and evaluated for isCapturable (63) with no SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, no pg_advisory_xact_lock, and no conditional state transition such as 'UPDATE order SET payment_status=<captured> WHERE payment_status=<authorized>' guarding entry; the network settle runs before any DB write (85), and updatePaymentStatus writes unconditionally (updatePaymentStatus.ts:31-36), so nothing at the DB layer rejects a stale second request, violating the 'captured at most once' invariant under concurrency.

trace.description: Handler reads only request.params.id and delegates to captureOrder(uuid) in services/captureOrder.ts.
`if (!statuses[order.payment_status]?.isCapturable)` evaluated from a lockless pre-transaction read (38-41, no FOR UPDATE); a competing request reads the same authorized status and also passes.
The network settle call runs before any DB write, outside any transaction or per-order advisory lock; two in-flight requests each reach their provider call.

insertOnUpdate('payment_transaction') (95) upserts on (transaction_id, payment_transaction_order_id), then updatePaymentStatus (113, updatePaymentStatus.ts:31-36) applies an unconditional UPDATE by order_id with no WHERE payment_status guard; no conditional transition rejects a second concurrent commit.

evidence.description: isCapturable gate read before any transaction or lock; order was loaded at 38-41 with no SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
factory.capture settles on the gateway before any DB write and without a per-order advisory lock (contrast createShipment.ts:90).

updatePaymentStatus commits the captured status after the gateway call via an unconditional UPDATE (updatePaymentStatus.ts:31-36); the upsert at 95 (ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE, postgres-query-builder src/index.ts:1134) and the absent conditional WHERE both permit a stale second request to commit.

blockers: Observing a double settlement requires two concurrent admin capture requests against the running app plus a live (or faithfully recording) gateway/mock with a barrier; no OS-enforced sandbox (network isolation, sanitized empty env, resource limits) exists in this environment, so runtime execution is disallowed.

Whether the second gateway settle moves funds is external provider behavior: Stripe rejects a second capture of an already-captured PaymentIntent while PayPal accepts multiple captures of one authorization and mints a new capture id per distinct PayPal-Request-Id; idempotency is not enforced by core.
Reproducing the exact race window depends on the real gateway call's network latency between the two in-flight requests.

validation_plan.local: Inside an OS-enforced sandbox (docker + network isolation): seed an order with payment_status = <method>_authorized and one authorization payment_transaction row; register a capture-handler mock that waits on a barrier, records each invocation, and returns a fresh transaction id; run two parallel captureOrder(uuid) calls and release the barrier only after both have entered factory.capture; assert two gateway calls were recorded and both capture rows / captured payment_status commit (demonstrates the lost update), then show a single settle + single ledger row when the fix gates on a conditional 'UPDATE order SET payment_status=<captured> WHERE payment_status=<authorized>' (or a pg_advisory_xact_lock).
validation_plan.deployment: Owner reviews the payment provider's capture logs for duplicate capture entries against the same authorization/PaymentIntent after near-simultaneous admin clicks (e.g., double-click) on the Capture button, and records the adapter's idempotency behavior (Stripe per-PaymentIntent; PayPal per-capture-id / PayPal-Request-Id).

title: Broken object-level authorization: public storefront GraphQL order(uuid) returns any order's PII with no ownership check
description: The storefront /graphql endpoint (route access: public) exposes the shared OMS order(uuid: String!): Order query with no ownership predicate. Query.order resolves the order via getOrdersBaseQuery() (a bare select().from('order') with no WHERE added except uuid equality) and does not compare the order's customer_id against any current-customer context. The shared Order.graphql type (merged into the public storefront schema because buildTypeDefs()/buildTypes.js exclude only *.admin.graphql types and buildResolvers(false) excludes only .admin.resolvers.*) carries server-side PII fields (customerEmail, customerFullName, userIp, shippingAddress, billingAddress with fullName/telephone/address1). The /graphql route's auth gate [getCurrentUser]auth.ts short-circuits on access === 'public', [auth]removeUser[graphql].ts clears context.user, and the middleware chain records no customer reference into the resolver. The intended invariant is documented in orderView/index.ts:9-13 ("the GraphQL order(uuid) resolver enforces that the order belongs to the current customer (storefront contract)") but no such enforcement exists in the resolver; the only customer-scoped sibling (Customer.orders, filters by order.customer_id) is not on this path. An anonymous caller supplying a target order's uuid is predicted to receive that order's full row and nested PII. Mitigating consideration: exploitation presumes knowledge of a target order uuid (v4, not inline-guessable), so the control absence is verified but real-world reachability depends on additional uuid-leak channels; the core missing-authorization defect is confirmed in source.
claimed_root_cause: Query.order in oms/graphql/types/Order/Order.resolvers.js:11-14 resolves an order by uuid alone (query.where('uuid','=',uuid)) over getOrdersBaseQuery() (select().from('order'), no ownership predicates); the shared (non-.admin.graphql) Order.graphql adds order(uuid:String!): Order to the storefront schema via buildTypes (ignoredExtensions excludes only '.admin.graphql') and buildResolvers(false); the /graphql route is access 'public' so [getCurrentUser]auth.ts short-circuits and [auth]removeUser[graphql].ts clears context.user; no middleware, resolver, or page enforces requestor ownership of the order.

trace.description: Method GET/POST route at path /graphql with access 'public'; registered to the frontStore router (loadModuleRoutes.js:48-63) so [getCurrentUser]auth.ts short-circuits at its public branch and no admin/customer session is required.

Gates only on request.isCustomerLoggedIn(); lines 9-13 comment explicitly assert the GraphQL order(uuid) resolver enforces ownership; line 27 stores the unvalidated URL param as orderUuid - the page relies on a resolver-side invariant that does not exist.
Sets context value 'user' to undefined on the storefront GraphQL route, leaving no principal in the request context for the resolver to bind an order to.
Invokes graphqlMiddleware with the storefront schema built by buildStoreFrontSchema.js (buildResolvers(false) + buildTypeDefs()) - the non-admin schema that includes the shared Order files.

Storefront type assembly excludes only files matching '.admin.graphql'; the shared oms Order.graphql (which defines order(uuid) at line 204) is merged into the public schema. buildResolvers(false) likewise excludes only '.admin.resolvers.*' plus '.ts'. Confirmed at buildStoreFrontSchema.js:5-9 vs buildSchema.js:5-9 (admin uses isAdmin=true).

The single Query.order resolver in the repo: getOrdersBaseQuery(); query.where('uuid','=',uuid); query.load(pool). No customer_id predicate, no context.customer check. Root parent/the third argument context are unused for access control.
select().from('order') with zero ownership predicates; the only WHERE ever added by the order(uuid) caller is uuid equality.

execute() runs the document against the storefront schema and responds 200 with data.data (lines 37-49); the unscoped Order row and nested PII (customerEmail/customerFullName/userIp/addresses/items/shipments) reach the caller. (validateSchema(schema, document) at line 22 is a separate fingerprint.)

evidence.description: extend type Query { order(uuid: String!): Order } lives in the shared (non-.admin.graphql) file, so it is merged into the public storefront schema.

PII on the public Order type: customerEmail (80), customerFullName (81), userIp (82); shippingAddress/billingAddress (75-76) resolve into OrderAddress fullName/postcode/telephone/address1/address2 (7-14).

Sibling control proving intended scoping exists only on Customer.orders (where('order.customer_id','=',customerId), lines 149-155) - not on the standalone order(uuid) query; repo-wide grep found no other Query.order resolver.
if (currentRoute?.access === 'public') { next(); return; } - the /graphql route bypasses all admin-session auth here.
Only loads a currentCustomer into request context when a valid session cookie/token exists; never rejects anonymous requests, and no resolver reads context.customer on the order(uuid) path.
Storefront customer page queries order(uuid: getContextValue("orderUuid")), demonstrating the public query is the customer-facing data path.
The admin Query extension adds only orders(filters:) list - confirming storefront order(uuid) originates solely from the shared Order.graphql.

blockers: No sandbox: the decisive end-to-end runtime fact (an anonymous POST to /graphql returns a victim order's PII) cannot be executed against a live instance, so confirmation is limited to the fully-deterministic source chain.

Exploitability presumes the caller can learn a target order uuid (uuid v4, not brute-forceable); the missing authorization control is verified in source, but reachability/impact depends on an un-verified uuid-leak channel - a severity/reachability nuance, not a refutation of the control defect.

validation_plan.local: Bounded fixture: boot Evershop in dev mode against a throwaway Postgres; create customer A with order A and customer B with order B. (1) Anonymous POST /graphql with { order(uuid: <orderB.uuid>) { orderNumber customerEmail customerFullName userIp shippingAddress { fullName telephone address1 } billingAddress { fullName } items { productName } } } - assert PII comes back (proves missing authZ). (2) Positive control: repeat with no/sessionless request and a second known uuid; identical result. (3) Negative control: verify Customer{ orders } under a customer token still filters by customer_id, and that a guest-accessible track-order path is NOT the vector used. Compare against the documented storefront contract (orderView/index.ts:9-13).
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed on staging/production: send the same anonymous /graphql order(uuid) query against a real checkout created by a test account; capture the 200 JSON body for PII fields; then confirm whether any deployment-specific middleware or extension resolver file (not on branch dev/18e0202) adds an ownership predicate that would alter the result, and inventory reachable uuid-leak channels (order emails, admin grid, referrers) to finalize severity.

title: Concurrent refund requests can all pass the remaining-amount gate and over-refund beyond the captured amount
description: createOrderRefund calls refundOrder, which loads the order, checks isRefundable, computes remainingRefundableMinorUnits from a pre-read of payment_transaction rows (refundOrder.ts:68-90), then calls the payment gateway (factory.refund, refundOrder.ts:94-99) and only afterwards recordRefund writes the refund row and updates payment status inside its own short transaction (recordRefund.ts:70-157). There is no per-order advisory lock and no conditional/atomic update pinning the remaining amount (updatePaymentStatus.ts:31-37 is an unconditional UPDATE with no guard), so two in-flight refunds can both read the same undiminished remainder, both invoke the gateway, and both record (idempotency dedupes only on the gateway-returned transactionId, recordRefund.ts:83-93) — the recorded refund total can exceed the captured amount.
claimed_root_cause: The refund gate is a check-then-act split across a network call and independent short transactions. Unlike the shipment path (pg_advisory_xact_lock at createShipment.ts:90 invoked at 571), the oms payment path never serializes per-order operations, and recordRefund.ts re-derives the totals from a fresh read (line 101) without atomically re-validating the captured ceiling — the summed total is used only to label full-vs-partial status, never to reject an over-cap refund.

trace.description: Number(request.body.amount) forwarded to refundOrder (route.json access 'private'; payloadSchema allows amount with max 2 decimals)
isRefundable check (line 62) and remainingRefundableMinorUnits (lines 81-85) computed from an unlocked pre-read of payment_transaction rows opened via pool; gate at 86 uses this stale remainder
Gateway refund (network I/O) is invoked outside any database transaction; a competing request can pass the same gate before either record commits

Re-reads transactions in a short mutation tx, computes totalRefunded = sumRefundedAmount(txns) + amount, inserts the refund row (110-123) and calls updatePaymentStatus (125) with no cap check against the captured amount; idempotency dedupes only on the gateway transactionId

evidence.description: Remaining amount gate: `!(amount > 0) || toMinorUnits(amount, currency) > remainingMinor` — evaluated from the un-locked pre-read, never re-checked after the gateway call
Gateway call happens while no DB write/transaction is held
Totals re-accumulated from a fresh read inside the mutation tx; no atomic decrement or ceiling assertion

Contrast control: the shipment path serializes per-order writes with `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext($1))` (taken at 571) — the refund/payment path has no per-order advisory lock or FOR UPDATE (grep confirms none in the oms payment path)

blockers: A real double-refund requires two concurrent admin requests against a database and a gateway that honors both refunds; no OS-enforced sandbox exists in this environment and runtime execution is disallowed, so this cannot be observed deterministically.

Whether the second gateway refund actually settles money — or whether the provider rejects simultaneous refunds exceeding the captured total (Stripe refunds are per-PaymentIntent; PayPal may mint a new refund) — is external provider behavior, not source-visible.
Exact refund row/status shape depends on which provider adapter (stripe/paypal) is active at runtime.

validation_plan.local: Non-destructive, in an OS-enforced sandbox only: seed a dummy order with one captured payment_transaction; substitute a recording mock for the payment factory that honors refunds and returns distinct transactionIds; fire two parallel refundOrder(amount=50% of capture) calls with a barrier such that both pass the gate before either records; assert either that the recorded refund sum exceeds 100% of the captured amount (race confirmed) or that the second request was rejected by a ceiling check (gate upheld). Either outcome discriminates the claim. This cannot run here: the environment has no OS-enforced sandbox and runtime execution is blocked by policy.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner can scan the payment-provider dashboard for any order whose cumulative refunded total exceeds its captured total after a double-click/concurrent-refund scenario, and confirm whether the active adapter serializes refunds.

title: Public POST /api/paypal/orders repoints a pending order's integration_order_id to a new PayPal order with no ownership or prior-binding guard
description: I independently re-read every cited file. paypalCreateOrder handler controls: route.json declares methods ['POST'], path '/paypal/orders', access 'public' (line 4), and scanForRoutes.js:47 mounts API routes under /api, so the endpoint is unauthenticated POST /api/paypal/orders. The auth gate passes public routes with next() ([getCurrentUser]auth.ts:18-21). payloadSchema.json requires only a string order_id with additionalProperties:true and the only route middleware is bodyParser, so there is no principal or cart token in the request. The order lookup (createOrder.ts:30-35) filters only uuid + payment_method='paypal' + payment_status='pending'; no session/cart/customer predicate and no check that integration_order_id is already bound. After PayPal returns an id, the handler unconditionally runs update('order').given({integration_order_id: data.id}).where('uuid','=',order_id) (lines 154-157) with no WHERE on the prior value. All downstream money paths trust the stored integration_order_id: paypalReturn/index.ts:27-28 requires uuid AND integration_order_id=token, then finalizePaypalOrder captures/authorizes against it (finalizePaypalOrder.ts:147-167); paypalCancel/index.ts:28-31 voids on it; reconcileAbandonedOrders.ts:21-22 reads /v2/checkout/orders/{integration_order_id} and cancelOrder (restock) on non-approved states. Amount integrity is separately present (buildPaypalAmount identity check, paypalPayload.ts:67-150; amount from order.grand_total). The unconditional binding overwrite is source-confirmed; what remains decisive and unobservable from source is whether a second public create can actually obtain a DISTINCT new PayPal order id for the same local order, given the handler always sends PayPal-Request-Id=order.uuid (line 145, intended as idempotency) and invoice_id=order.order_number (line 73), or whether PayPal's idempotency returns the original id and therefore neutralizes the repoint.
claimed_root_cause: The PayPal order-mint boundary lacks an ownership predicate AND an already-bound guard: the public /api/paypal/orders endpoint overwrites order.integration_order_id unconditionally, letting any uuid-knower re-route the order's payment leg to a different PayPal order; protection against re-binding is delegated entirely to PayPal-side idempotency (PayPal-Request-Id / invoice_id) rather than enforced in the local write.

trace.description: Route declares methods ['POST'], path '/paypal/orders', access 'public'; API routes are mounted under /api by scanForRoutes.js:47, and the global [getCurrentUser] auth gate passes public routes with next() (auth.ts:18-21), so any unauthenticated caller reaches the handler.

Order lookup: .where('uuid','=',order_id).and('payment_method','=','paypal').and('payment_status','=','pending') (lines 32-35). No session/cart/customer ownership predicate and no check that the order is not already bound to a PayPal order; payloadSchema.json requires only order_id.

PayPal create-order issued with purchase_units amount derived server-side from order.grand_total (identity-checked by buildPaypalAmount, paypalPayload.ts:67-150), invoice_id=order.order_number (line 73) and PayPal-Request-Id=order.uuid (line 145); the server-side amount closes the amount dimension, but the request/response identity is keyed to fixed local values, not to any caller principal.

await update('order').given({ integration_order_id: data.id }).where('uuid','=',order_id).execute(pool) (lines 154-157): overwrites any prior integration_order_id unconditionally with no guard on the current value and no ownership predicate.

Return leg selects .where('uuid','=',order_id).and('integration_order_id','=',paypalToken) (lines 27-28); after a repoint, the browser token of the repointed (attacker) PayPal order is accepted for the victim order and finalizePaypalOrder (finalizePaypalOrder.ts:147-167) captures/authorizes against the repointed order id.

Cron GETs /v2/checkout/orders/{order.integration_order_id} (line 22) for every pending paypal order past TTL: captures an APPROVED/COMPLETED repointed order via finalizePaypalOrderOrFail (line 44) or cancels the victim order with restock (cancelOrder) when the repointed order is not approved or no longer exists (lines 25-31, 47-53).

Cancel leg selects .where('integration_order_id','=',paypalToken).and('uuid','=',order_id).and('payment_method','=','paypal').and('payment_status','=','pending') (lines 28-31) and cancels the order (money path cancelOrder, line 37); its trusted key is the repointed integration_order_id.

evidence.description: Unconditional overwrite of integration_order_id - update('order').given({ integration_order_id: data.id }).where('uuid','=',order_id), no WHERE on the prior binding value and no pre-existing-binding check in the preceding select (lines 30-35).
Lookup filters only uuid + payment_method='paypal' + payment_status='pending' (lines 32-35); owner identity (session/cart/customer) is never consulted.
access 'public' plus scanForRoutes.js:47 mounting under /api makes the binding-overwrite reachable by any unauthenticated caller; the auth middleware passes public routes (auth.ts:18-21).
Only 'order_id' (string) is required and additionalProperties:true - no ownership token, cart id, or customer binding is accepted or checked.
The trusted binding is .and('integration_order_id','=',paypalToken) (line 28); its integrity is exactly what the unguarded repoint violates, and finalizePaypalOrder acts on that stored id.
finalizePaypalOrderOrFail acts on the stored order.integration_order_id (read at line 22) with no re-validation against the buyer's original instrument.

PayPal-Request-Id is always order.uuid (line 145) and invoice_id always order.order_number (line 73): re-binding protection is delegated to PayPal's idempotency/dedup behavior, a runtime fact that determines whether a second create returns the original id (no repoint) or a distinct new id (repoint).

blockers: No OS-enforced sandbox: cannot run a local fixture proving a second unauthenticated POST actually repoints the order row to a new PayPal order id (NO SANDBOX RULE); a local mock's idempotency semantics would be our own, not PayPal's.

Decisive fact is a PayPal sandbox runtime observation: a second create for the same local order always sends fixed PayPal-Request-Id=order.uuid (createOrder.ts:145) and invoice_id=order.order_number (line 73); whether PayPal returns the original order id (idempotent -> update is a no-op, no repoint) or mints a different new order id across statuses/time must be observed against the real /v2/checkout/orders API with real merchant credentials.
Cross-principal knowledge of the pending paypal order uuid depends on peer-owned IDOR disclosure units (checkout createOrder / Query.order / getCartByUUID), which need their own validation.

Practical window: reconcileAbandonedOrders.ts:64-67 cancels pending paypal orders after the configured TTL (default 6h), so the order stays bindable only within that window; whether it overlaps a period in which PayPal's idempotency has lapsed or returns a new id for re-created orders is a deployment fact.

validation_plan.local: Sandboxed fixture with a mocked PayPal adapter that REFUSES idempotency (mints a fresh order id per call): seed one pending paypal order O (payment_method='paypal', payment_status='pending'); POST /api/paypal/orders twice from two different caller identities with the same order_id; assert the second call returns its own paypalOrderId/approveUrl and that order.integration_order_id changed to the second id, then assert paypalReturn?order_id=O&token=<first order id> now redirects to homepage. Success here only proves the handler-side write is unconditional (already visible in source); it cannot establish the real-world repoint because PayPal's real idempotency response is not modeled.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed on a real PayPal sandbox (no production traffic): create local order O; as buyer identity A, POST /api/paypal/orders and let A reach PayPal; then from identity B POST /api/paypal/orders for the same O and record whether PayPal returns a new distinct order id or replays A's id (this is the decisive fact). If a distinct id is returned, complete payment via B's approval URL and verify the capture is recorded against O with B's order id, demonstrating the repointed binding steers the money leg; if PayPal replays A's id, record that the overwrite is a no-op and re-assess exploitability.

title: Public admin/customer JWT-mint endpoints run bcrypt credential checks under the permissive api tier (120/min) instead of the strict auth tier (8/15min), with a locale-prefixed spelling escaping to the page tier (300/min)
description: POST /api/user/tokens (admin JWT mint, getUserToken) and POST /api/customer/tokens (customer JWT mint, getCustomerToken) are access:public API routes that perform the same email + bcrypt.compareSync password check as the page login endpoints (/admin/user/login, /customer/login), but rateLimit.ts classifies them to the 'api' tier (120 req/60s) rather than the 'auth' tier (8 req/15min). AUTH_POST_PATHS (rateLimit.ts:48-54) enumerates only /customer/login, /admin/user/login, /api/customers, /api/customers/reset-password, /api/customers/password, and the unit test (rateLimit.test.ts:17-23) asserts classification only for those. Over a 15-minute window the api tier admits ~1800 attempts from one IP vs 8 for auth (~225x larger per-IP budget; the hunter's quoted '~22.5x' is an order of magnitude off). Because classifyRequest applies isApiPath to the raw path while route resolution consumes the locale-stripped request.localePath (rateLimiter is mounted before the locale-strip middleware), a prefixed spelling like POST /fr/api/user/tokens (fr an enabled non-default locale) is routed to the same handler but classified 'page' tier (300/60s) — a further 2.5x. The tier-classification gap is fully source-confirmed; the actual account-compromise outcome requires runtime observation (explicitly blocked in this environment).

title: Per-IP rate-limit buckets are attacker-influenceable when TRUST_PROXY_HOPS defaults to 1 and docker-compose publishes the app directly without a proxy
description: getTrustProxyHops() returns 1 whenever TRUST_PROXY_HOPS is unset/empty/invalid, and app.set('trust proxy', getTrustProxyHops()) installs that numeric hop count. Express trust-proxy semantics with a numeric value trust the direct socket peer and derive req.ip from the left-most (first client-supplied) X-Forwarded-For entry when that peer is not actually an overwriting proxy. The pinned express-rate-limit 8.7.0 MemoryStore keys its per-IP buckets on req.ip (default keyGenerator), and the rateLimiter is mounted before session/locale/DB work for every non-test request. In the repo's only maintained deployment artifact (docker-compose.yml) the app port 3000 is published directly to the host (only services: app + postgres, no proxy container) and TRUST_PROXY_HOPS is never set. An unauthenticated caller can therefore (a) rotate X-Forwarded-For to escape any per-IP quota (page 300/60s, api 120/60s, auth 8/15min), removing the only source-visible anti-DoS and brute-force guard on login/JWT/token endpoints, and (b) pin a victim IP to consume its quota (e.g. burn the victim's 8/15-min auth attempts). Route-level tier gaps (JWT-mint endpoints on the looser api tier) amplify this. Whether the vector is live depends on the real production edge rewriting/normalizing X-Forwarded-For in front of the app, which is not observable from source.
claimed_root_cause: getTrustProxyHops() returns 1 for any unset/empty/invalid TRUST_PROXY_HOPS; Express numeric trust-proxy semantics make a directly-connected, non-loopback internet client the single trusted hop, so the first client-supplied X-Forwarded-For value becomes req.ip; express-rate-limit 8.7.0 keys its MemoryStore per-IP buckets on req.ip via the default keyGenerator; the compose deployment exposes the app directly on 0.0.0.0:3000 with no in-repo reverse proxy and never configures the variable.

trace.description: TRUST_PROXY_HOPS unset/empty/invalid -> returns 1 hop trusted; file comment (lines 13-15) documents that a too-high hop count lets a client spoof X-Forwarded-For to dodge limits and that the fallback is 1.
app.set('trust proxy', getTrustProxyHops()) — numeric 1 makes the directly-connected peer the trusted hop and the first client-supplied X-Forwarded-For entry authoritative for req.ip.

limiters[page|api|auth] are built once at module load; express-rate-limit 8.7.0 default keyGenerator returns req.ip, so the per-IP bucket equals the spoofed (or victim-supplied) X-Forwarded-For value under trust proxy 1.
rateLimiter mounted before session/locale/DB work for all requests when NODE_ENV !== 'test'; classifyRequest selects the tier then the per-IP MemoryStore applies.

app ports 3000:3000 published (0.0.0.0) with no proxy service on the myevershop network and no TRUST_PROXY_HOPS/edge normalization set; the maintained compose render therefore exposes the arbitrary internet peer as the single trusted proxy hop.

evidence.description: Raw undefined/empty (and non-integer/negative) -> return 1; numeric count drives Express trust proxy (pinned express 4.22.2 per package-lock).
trust proxy set centrally from TRUST_PROXY_HOPS via getTrustProxyHops().
RULES: page 300/60s (line 18), api 120/60s (line 20), auth 8/15min (line 22) — per-IP tiers.
MemoryStore limiters constructed once and keyed on req.ip via express-rate-limit v8 default keyGenerator (pinned 8.7.0 per package-lock).
rateLimiter mounted for every request when NODE_ENV !== 'test', before session/locale/DB (lines 90, 107+).
app: ports - 3000:3000, no proxy container on the myevershop network; only app + database services; TRUST_PROXY_HOPS never set; DB published 5432:5432.

blockers: Deployed topology is not observable from source: whether production actually runs behind a real reverse proxy/edge (nginx, ALB, CDN) or WAF that rewrites/strips client-supplied X-Forwarded-For before the app decides whether a spoofed XFF can reach req.ip. Source only proves the compose render exposes the app directly with trust proxy 1.

No OS-enforced sandbox (no external-network isolation, sanitized env, or resource limits) is available, so the deterministic-but-executed behavior of the pinned Express 4.22.2 / express-rate-limit 8.7.0 stack (req.ip derived from the first X-Forwarded-For entry under numeric trust=1 when the peer is an arbitrary internet client; per-IP 429 bucket keying) was not demonstrated with a bounded local run.

validation_plan.local: In an OS-enforced offline sandbox with the pinned package-lock, boot the app with TRUST_PROXY_HOPS unset bound to :3000; send 10 POST /admin/user/login requests each carrying a distinct X-Forwarded-For: <valid IP> and assert no 429 is returned (auth tier 8/15min bypassed), reading the RateLimit-* headers to confirm the per-IP bucket key changed; repeat the same loop with TRUST_PROXY_HOPS=0 and assert XFF no longer alters req.ip (bucket stays on the socket IP). Use dummy credentials only; no external network.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner confirms whether the production edge rewrites/normalizes X-Forwarded-For, and whether TRUST_PROXY_HOPS equals the real proxy depth (0 for direct exposure, 1+ for proxy chains); also record any firewall/WAF layer in front of 0.0.0.0:3000. If a single overwriting proxy fronts the app, the spoof vector is closed at that boundary.

title: Public Stripe payment-intent minting is bound only to a client-supplied order uuid (missing object-level authorization)
description: POST /api/stripe/paymentIntents is declared public, the authentication middleware short-circuits public routes, and the handler loads the order using only a client-supplied order_id filtered by uuid, payment_method='stripe', payment_status='pending' - with no customer/session/cart ownership predicate. The handler then creates a real Stripe PaymentIntent for that order and returns its client_secret to the unauthenticated caller. Any caller who merely knows an order uuid can mint payment intents against arbitrary pending orders; the same uuid is later the sole binding used by the webhook to drive order payment-state transitions (payment_intent.canceled -> order 'canceled'). Amount-integrity controls do exist and are confirmed (amount comes from the server-side order row, never the request body; webhook rejects money-in unless paymentIntentMatchesOrder), so the record stays scoped to this ownership gap.
claimed_root_cause: The stripe payment-intent minting boundary trusts a client-supplied order_id with no ownership binding: the route is public (route.json access:'public'), the API credential gate explicitly skips public routes ([getCurrentUser]auth.ts:18-21), and the handler's order select has no principal predicate (createPaymentIntent.ts:31-34), so the returned client_secret and the order's payment-state machine are reachable by any uuid-knower.

trace.description: route declared {"methods":["POST"],"path":"/stripe/paymentIntents","access":"public"}; scanForRoutes.js:47 prefixes API routes with /api and loadModuleRoutes.js:50 scans the module api folder, mounting it at /api/stripe/paymentIntents.
if (currentRoute?.access === 'public') { next(); return; } - the credential/role gate is bypassed for public routes, so the handler runs without any authenticated principal.
const { order_id } = request.body; payloadSchema.json:11 requires plain-string cart_id and order_id with additionalProperties:true; cart_id is never used by the handler.

select().from('order').where('uuid','=',order_id).and('payment_method','=','stripe').and('payment_status','=','pending').load(pool) - predicates are only uuid/method/status; no customer, session, or cart ownership check (lines 29-34).

stripe.paymentIntents.create({ amount: toStripeMinorUnit(order.grand_total, order.currency), currency: order.currency, metadata: { order_id: order.uuid }, ... }) - amount and currency are taken from the server-owned order row (not the body); metadata order_id is the order's own uuid, set server-side.
response.json({ data: { clientSecret: paymentIntent.client_secret } }) - the live client_secret is returned to the unauthenticated caller.

order resolved solely from paymentIntent.metadata?.order_id via loadOrderByUuidForUpdate; in the payment_intent.canceled branch (lines 303-309) any non-canceled order with that uuid is moved to 'canceled' (guarded only by order.payment_status !== 'canceled'). Note: producing the canceled event requires canceling the intent on Stripe's side.

evidence.description: Order fetch has no principal predicate: only uuid, payment_method='stripe', payment_status='pending'; no join/binding to the requesting customer, session, or cart.
order_id read directly from request.body; payloadSchema.json:11 requires {cart_id, order_id} with additionalProperties:true and the handler ignores cart_id.
clientSecret returned to the caller with no ownership verification.
access "public" confirmed; mounted at POST /api/stripe/paymentIntents (scanForRoutes.js:47).
public-route shortcut: next(); return; bypasses the admin credential + role gate.
payment_intent.canceled branch: if (order.payment_status !== 'canceled') updatePaymentStatus(..., 'canceled') - no other guard.
money-in integrity control confirmed present: paymentIntentMatchesOrder(order, paymentIntent) rejects amount/currency mismatch before any status change (stripeAmount.ts:20-29).
stripe_captured isCancelable:false (line 25) confirmed, consistent with the claimed payment-state framing.
toStripeMinorUnit used for the intent amount from the order row, not the body - amount integrity control confirmed.

blockers: No sandbox is available, so the end-to-end mint/state-change path cannot be exercised against a real Postgres order row + Stripe API in this read-only review.

Stripe external behavior is outside source: producing a payment_intent.canceled delivery requires the intent to be canceled on Stripe's side; per Stripe's API cancellation requires the account secret key, so the webhook canceled-branch sink (webhook.ts:303-309) may be unreachable by an attacker holding only the returned client_secret - the money-in transitions fire only if the attacker actually pays the full order amount from their own card.
Webhook impact depends on deployment (endpoint secret configured, events enabled) and on real delivery behavior - not observable from source.

Real-world severity (attacker-funded fulfillment of arbitrary pending orders, duplicate payment_transaction rows re-emitting order_placed when a victim and attacker both pay) requires a live merchant Stripe account to confirm.
